'''Paul Burgan Weisz''' (July 2, 1919 – September 25, 2012) was a Czechoslovak-born American [[chemist]], noted for his work on solid [[catalyst]]s, which had a major impact on [[petroleum refining]].

==Life==
Weisz was born July 2, 1919, in [[Plzeň]], [[Czechoslovakia]], the son of Alexander and Amalia Weisz. They moved to [[Berlin]] and finally emigrated to the [[United States]] in 1939.<ref name=Degnan>{{cite book |last=Degnan, Jr |first=Thomas |date=2015 |title=Memorial Tributes, Volume 19 |url=https://www.nap.edu/read/21785/chapter/56 |publisher=National Academies Press |pages=311–316 |isbn=978-0-309-37720-1 |access-date=2018-09-17 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180728071309/https://www.nap.edu/read/21785/chapter/56 |archive-date=2018-07-28 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name=CEN>{{cite journal |last1=Ainsworth |first1=Susan |date=November 26, 2012 |title=Paul B Weisz |url=https://cen.acs.org/articles/90/i48/Paul-B-Weisz.html |journal=Chemical & Engineering News |volume=90 |issue=48 |pages=42 |access-date=September 10, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180917181814/https://cen.acs.org/articles/90/i48/Paul-B-Weisz.html |archive-date=September 17, 2018 |url-status=live }}</ref>
He married and was survived by his wife, Rhoda, his son, Randy, and his daughter, Ingrid.
He died on September 25, 2012, in [[State College, Pennsylvania]].<ref name=CEN/>

==Education==
Weisz studied physics at the [[Technische Hochschule]] in Charlottenburg (now [[Technische Universität Berlin]]) and then at the [[Alabama Polytechnic Institute]], where he received a B.S. degree in 1940. He took a sabbatical from work and gained a doctorate at [[ETH Zurich]] in 1966.<ref name=Degnan/><ref name=CEN/>

==Work==
Weisz produced 91 US patents and more than 180 papers, many related to [[diffusion]] behavior, which he applied to solid catalysts, [[dyeing]], and the movement of chemicals in cells.<ref name=Degnan/>

===Early career===
While studying in Berlin, he also worked on [[Geiger counter]] instrumentation and [[cosmic ray]] measurements at the Institute of Cosmic Radiation Research.  After graduating in the US, he carried out further work in these fields at the [[Bartol Research Institute|Bartol Research Foundation]] of the [[Franklin Institute]] and was seconded to [[MIT]] to help develop a long-range radio navigation system, [[LORAN]].  He also taught part-time at [[Swarthmore College]].<ref name=Oral>{{cite web |url=https://oh.sciencehistory.org/oral-histories/weisz-paul-b |title=Paul B. Weisz |last=Bohning |first=James |website=oh.sciencehistory.org |publisher=Science History Institute Center for Oral History |access-date=September 17, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181201001201/https://oh.sciencehistory.org/oral-histories/weisz-paul-b |archive-date=December 1, 2018 |url-status=live }}</ref>

===Mobil===
In 1946, he joined [[Mobil]] as a Research Assistant, turning his attention to diffusion and catalysis, eventually rising to become Manager of the Central Research Laboratory, and staying there until his retirement in 1984.<ref name=Degnan/><ref name=Oral/>  It was there that he carried out the work which made him most famous. The development of shape-selective catalysts revolutionized many petroleum refining and chemical processes.<ref name=CEN/>  A 1960 paper, "Intracrystalline and Molecular-Shape-Selective Catalysis by Zeolite Salts",<ref name=Weisz1>{{cite journal |last1=Weisz |first1=P. B. |last2=Frilette |first2=V. J. |date=1960 |title=Intracrystalline and Molecular-Shape-Selective Catalysis by Zeolite Salts |journal=Journal of Physical Chemistry |volume=64 |issue=3 |pages=382 |doi=10.1021/j100832a513 }}</ref> coauthored with Vince Frilette, a Mobil colleague,  became the foundation of shape-selective catalysis (which accelerated certain chemical reactions, but only for molecules of particular shape) and one of his most widely cited papers. Processes based on this and subsequent work were first commercialized in the early 1960s.<ref name=Degnan/>

The company permitted him a sabbatical period from 1964 to 1966 at ETH Zurich, where he earned a doctorate, setting the foundation for some of the fundamental laws of diffusion in dyeing.<ref name=Degnan/>

===Academic career===
From 1974 to 1976, he was a [[visiting professor]] at [[Princeton University]]. From 1983 on, he was a [[distinguished professor]] of [[Chemical engineering|chemical]] and [[Biological engineering|bio-engineering]] at the University of Pennsylvania. Since 1993, he has been an [[adjunct professor]] in [[chemical engineering]] at [[Pennsylvania State University]].<ref name=Oral/>  In this period, he applied chemical and physical principles to biomedical research, including work with [[Madeleine M. Joullié]] on the synthesis of a molecule equivalent to [[heparin]] which avoided the dangerous side-effects of the natural molecule.<ref name=Degnan/>

==Honors==
*1972 [[E. V. Murphree Award in Industrial and Engineering Chemistry]], American Chemical Society<ref name=Degnan/><ref name=Oral/>
*1974 Pioneer Award, American Institute of Chemists<ref name=Degnan/><ref name=Oral/>
*1977 Leo Friend Award, American Chemical Society<ref name=Degnan/><ref name=Oral/>
*1977 Elected member, US [[National Academy of Engineering]] for “Contributions in pioneering the use of molecular sieves as cracking catalysts for petroleum hydrocarbons.”<ref name=Degnan/><ref name=Oral/>
*1978 R. H. Wilhelm Award, [[American Institute of Chemical Engineers]]<ref name=Degnan/><ref name=Oral/>
*1980 Honorary Doctorate (ScD, technological science), ETH Zurich<ref name=Degnan/>
*1983 [[Lavoisier Medal]], [[Société Chimique de France]]<ref name=Degnan/><ref name=Oral/>
*1983 Langmuir Distinguished Lecturer Award, American Chemical Society<ref name=Degnan/><ref name=Oral/>
*1985 [[Perkin Medal]], [[Society of Chemical Industry]]<ref name=Degnan/><ref name=Oral/>
*1986 Chemistry of Contemporary Technological Problems Award, American Chemical Society<ref name=Degnan/><ref name=Oral/>
*1987 Carothers Award, American Chemical Society<ref name=Degnan/><ref name=Oral/>
*1988 DGKM Kollegium Award (Germany)<ref name=Degnan/><ref name=Oral/>
*1992 US [[National Medal of Technology and Innovation]] "For his basic discoveries and management in the field of zeolite catalysis, in conjunction with his colleagues at Mobil Corporation, leading to chemical and petroleum technologies now producing products valued at billions of dollars per year."<ref name=NSTMF>{{cite web |url=https://www.nationalmedals.org/laureates/paul-b-weisz |title=Paul B. Weisz |author=<!--Not stated--> |website=www.nationalmedals.org |publisher=National Science and Technology Medals Foundation |access-date=September 17, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180917182246/https://www.nationalmedals.org/laureates/paul-b-weisz |archive-date=September 17, 2018 |url-status=live }}</ref>
